Asks again whether Rav Pappa's ruling is not obvious.
Needed where sellers add extra onions after weighing, so the place still counts as one selling onions by weight.
Restates the mishna's incident of the mother of Yirmatya paying her daughter's weight in gold.
Asks whether the incident is cited to contradict the mishna's earlier rule about silver and gold.
The mishna is incomplete: a distinguished person pays according to his status, as the wealthy mother of Yirmatya did in gold.
Rav Yehuda rules that one who vows his height gives a thick unbendable rod, while full height allows a thin bendable rod.
Objects from a baraita that says even one who vows full height gives a thick rod that cannot be bent.
Rav Yehuda follows Rabbi Akiva, who infers from superfluous wording, as in the house-sale case about access paths.
Raises a dilemma: if one vows his stature, what is the halakha?

ranges.en: Asks the halakha for vows about one's width, sitting, thickness and girth, and leaves these dilemmas unresolved.
Restates the mishna's case of one who vows the weight of his forearm and how the weight is ascertained.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says to fill a barrel with water and insert the forearm or leg, weighing the donkey flesh displaced.
Supports the donkey-flesh method with a verse comparing human flesh to the flesh of donkeys.
Rabbi Yosei objects that displacement measures volume, so matching flesh, sinews and bones to a person's body is impossible.
Rabbi Yehuda replies that one estimates the matching amounts.
Rabbi Yosei answers that if one only estimates, one should estimate the forearm's weight directly.
Rabbi Yehuda holds we do what is possible for precision, and the forearm term means up to the elbow.
A contradicting baraita says the hands and feet sanctified in the Temple are up to the wrist, not the elbow.
The Torah's yad means up to the wrist, but vows follow ordinary speech, where yad means the forearm.
Objects that the word yad in the phylacteries verse refers to the biceps area, which would change the reading.
Torah yad includes the biceps area, vows follow common usage, and the Temple rule is a received tradition up to the wrist.
Tosefta: a vow of the leg means the leg until the knee, as the term regel is defined.
A baraita reads the pilgrimage verse regalim as excluding those with artificial legs, which suggests regel means the foot.
Regel in the Torah means the foot below the ankle, while vows follow ordinary speech where regel means up to the knee.
Objects from the halitza mishna, where a yavam missing part of his leg still allows halitza from the knee down.
The verse says from upon the foot, so halitza above the foot is valid, and the ankle bone is treated as part of the foot.
Mishna: for a vow of one's forearm's assessment, the court values him with and without it and he pays the difference.
Asks how the court actually assesses such a person.
Rava says the court uses the damages assessment method, valuing the injured party as a slave before and after the injury.
Abaye objects that a damaged person is depreciated in value, while a vower's own value is intact, so the two cases differ.
Abaye proposes assessing how much more a buyer pays for a slave working with two hands than with one.
Asks what the one-hand slave case is, since a severed hand would make it the same as Rava's damages method.
Rather, the case is a slave whose one hand is reserved in his bill of sale for the first owner.
Rava raises a dilemma: if assessed by three judges for damages and then he says his assessment is incumbent, must it be done by ten.
Asks whether an assessment by ten is needed again when he repeats his vow after already being assessed by the court.
Asks the same dilemma when the court has not yet assessed him and he repeats his vow before assessment.

ranges.en: Asks whether one who vows in sequence is assessed once for a double vow or assessed twice.
Asks whether saying twice at once counts as a sequential vow, requiring two assessments.
Asks whether a court assessment made on its own counts as an assessment for a vow, or intent is needed.
Proposes resolving one dilemma from the mishna: the heirs owe nothing, since the dead have no monetary value.
If a court assessment made on its own counted, the mishna would be pointless, so intent is needed for the assessment.
Rejects that resolution: a court assessment before the vow is an actual assessment, unlike a vow made without one.
Mishna: a vow of valuation binds heirs, but a vow of assessment does not; limbs carry no valuation, only the whole self.
Mishna: for halves, half the valuation is given for half, but half of oneself means the whole assessment, since the soul is involved.
Mishna: if the object of a vow dies, the heirs of a vow of valuation pay, but a vow of assessment is not payable.
Baraita: vows of assessment apply to animals and birds and are not limited by means, unlike valuations; the death rules differ.
Infers from the baraita that a Torah-based oral loan is collected from heirs, as the valuation is an obligation to the Temple.
Rejects that inference: the valuation here is a debt written in the Torah, which is different from an oral loan.
Objects that if a Torah obligation counts as written, then any Torah loan would be as binding as a signed document.
Limits the baraita to one who stood in judgment and was obligated by the court before death, like a written document.
Asks why, in that case, the heirs of a vow of assessment do not pay, since the court ruling would also apply.
Rav Giddel says in Rav's name that a person who vows the valuation of a forearm or leg still must give the assessment.
Asks how that conflicts with the mishna that says he has said nothing.
The mishna follows the Sages, who say nothing, while Rabbi Meir holds he must give the assessment, since he did not speak for naught.
Asks why Rav Giddel repeats a point already said, that a vow of a vessel's valuation requires its assessment.
Repeated because one might think the vessel case is special, while a vow about a forearm or leg was made in error.
Mishna: a vow of the valuation of one's head or liver means giving the valuation of one's entire self.
The verse says valuations of living people, and the principle includes a leg cut from above the knee, which is fatal.
Mishna: a vow of half one's valuation gives half the valuation.
Baraita: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says one who vows half the valuation is flogged and gives the full valuation.
Asks why such a person is flogged if he committed no sin.
Rav Pappa says it is a rabbinic decree, to avoid confusion with a vow of half of oneself, which requires the full value.
Mishna: a vow of half one's assessment gives half, but a vow of half of oneself gives the assessment of the entire self.
Asks the reason for applying the same rule to assessments as to valuations.
The verse joins vow and valuation, and the principle covers a leg cut from above the knee, so assessment follows the same rule.
Baraita: Rabbi Meir says one who vows half a vessel's assessment gives half, while the Sages say he has said nothing.
Rava became ill and Abaye visited; they accept Rabbi Meir's principle that one does not speak for naught.
Asks what the Sages hold, since on either view the vessel rule would not follow in the same way.
The Sages follow Rabbi Meir and also Rabbi Shimon, who exempts a vow of an unsuitable item not donated in the usual way.
Mishna: a vow of valuation of so-and-so makes the vower's heirs pay if the vower dies, but the object's death changes nothing.
Asks what case the mishna's clause refers to, and why it duplicates the earlier clause.
The repetition is needed to teach the latter clause, about a vow of the assessment of so-and-so, where the heirs must pay.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Lest one think the property is not liened when no assessment was made, the mishna teaches that standing in judgment suffices.
Mishna: a vow to offer a consecrated bull or house exempts one if it dies or collapses, but a vow to give it obligates payment.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Rav explains the mishna: a vow to give the bull's monetary value is what creates liability on its death.
Objects from a baraita that treats the bull as consecrated and makes the vower liable on loss even without a monetary vow.
Replies that the baraita too speaks of a monetary value vow, so it matches the mishna.
Objects that the latter clause of the baraita shows the first clause does not mean monetary value, since sale proceeds are owed.
Both clauses refer to a monetary-value vow: one consecrates the bull for its value, the other consecrates future sale proceeds.
Asks how one can consecrate sale proceeds that do not yet exist, since a person cannot consecrate what has not come into the world.
Rav Yehuda says Rav holds this is Rabbi Meir's view, who allows consecrating what has not yet come into the world; the story is told two ways.
Brings a baraita on a house rented and found leprous to show the same dispute arises in a different context.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: if the house's renter consecrates it, the rent he has already paid is lost to the Temple treasury.
Asks how a renter can consecrate a house, since the verse ties consecration to one's own house.
Explains the baraita means the landlord consecrates the house, and the tenant pays the rent to the treasury.
Asks how the tenant can live in consecrated property and why the rent becomes non-sacred once he misuses it.
The landlord's words refer to future rent, so the case follows Rabbi Meir, who allows consecrating what is not yet in the world.
Mishna: those owing valuations have their property repossessed; sin and guilt offerings are not, while burnt and peace offerings are.
Rav Pappa says the court sometimes repossesses for sin offerings and sometimes not for burnt offerings.
Cites the nazirite rule from Nazir 45a, where the sin offering may be neglected, so the court repossesses for it.
The court does not repossess for a woman's burnt offering after childbirth, since she must bring it before eating sacrifices.
Asks why the verse lists the burnt offering before the sin offering, given Rava's view that this is only the order of reading.
The exception is the burnt offering of a leper, which, like his sin and guilt offerings, must be brought for full purity, per Rabbi Yishmael.
Restates the mishna: atonement requires one's own consent, yet the court coerces the offerer until he says he wants to.
Baraita: the verse says he shall sacrifice it, showing coercion, and of his volition, showing consent.
Asks how these two verse readings are reconciled with the mishna's rule.
Shmuel says a burnt offering requires the consent of the one receiving atonement, as the verse of volition shows.
Asks what Shmuel adds, since the mishna already says atonement needs the offerer's own volition.
Shmuel's point is needed for a burnt offering separated from another person's property, where consent is still required.
Objects from a baraita about a vow to bring the sin or guilt offering of another person.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: if one vows another's burnt offering and does it with that person's consent, the obligation is fulfilled; without consent, it is not.
Baraita: a vow to bring another's burnt or peace offering fulfills the obligation whether or not he consents.
Shmuel says the baraita with no consent refers to the time of atonement, while his consent is needed when the animal is set apart.
Ulla's position: consent for sin and guilt offerings is needed when the animal is set apart, but for all offerings it is needed at atonement.
A baraita requiring consent for every offering is difficult for both Shmuel's and Ulla's positions.
Shmuel and Ulla read the baraitot in different times; Rav Pappa says they do not conflict, and the summary is needed to clarify Shmuel.
Mishna on divorce: one coerced to divorce says he wants to; Rav Sheshet says a prior declaration of coercion cancels the bill.
Asks whether Rav Sheshet's ruling is not obvious.
Needed where he later gives the bill voluntarily without retracting his declaration; the mishna's wording shows retraction is required.
Mishna: the appraisal of orphans' property is proclaimed for thirty days, and consecrated property for sixty, morning and evening.
Asks why the proclamation is made specifically in the morning and in the evening.
Rav says morning is when workers leave for the fields and evening when they return, so a buyer can ask them to inspect the property.
A baraita states the same timing and periods, confirming the explanation.
Baraita: the proclaimer describes the field and its yield, and says it is sold to pay a wife's marriage contract or a creditor.
Asks why the proclaimer must state the purpose of the sale, to the wife or to the creditor.
Some buyers prefer dealing with a creditor, who takes any coins, and others prefer a wife, who accepts payment in installments.

ranges.en: Baraita gives three opinions on the proclamation period; Rav Hisda reports Avimi's halakha of sixty days for orphans' property.
Rav Naham bar Yitzhak questions Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin on whether the sixty days apply to orphans or consecrated property.
Objects that Rabbi Meir, whose view the speaker follows, actually says thirty days for orphans' property.
Avimi explains: thirty days of consecutive proclamations, or sixty days when announced only twice weekly, so people hear of the sale.
Rav Asi holds the court acts for orphans only when interest consumes their property; Rabbi Yohanan adds a marriage contract or interest-bearing note.
Asks why Rav Asi does not allow the court to pay a marriage contract, and why Rabbi Yohanan thinks it is needed.
Objects that the mishna's sixty and thirty day rule for a gentile or Jewish creditor contradicts both Rav Asi and Rabbi Yohanan.
Rabbi Yohanan's case is a widow who claims her marriage contract in court, which by Shmuel's ruling ends her sustenance from the estate.
Asks why the court should not simply delay payment to the widow until the orphans reach majority, since they lose nothing by waiting.
The mishna means a gentile creditor who agreed to Jewish law, so he will wait thirty days to collect.
Asks why such a creditor would not also be barred from taking interest under Jewish law.
Cites Gittin 48b that orphans' land is sold only from the lowest quality, and presses the same contradiction against Rav Asi.
Rabbi Yohanan follows Rabbi Meir: a marriage contract is paid in middling land, and from orphans it is paid in inferior land.
Asks again how the mishna fits Rav Asi, and why the gentile creditor would not refuse interest.
A baraita on proclamations for a marriage contract or a creditor is a difficulty for Rav Asi's view.
Here the obligor admitted he had not yet paid, so the court collects from orphans without delay in all these cases.
Mareimar collected a divorced woman's marriage contract from orphans' property, and Ravina challenged him.
Ravina objects that Rav Yehuda's report of Rav Asi shows that the court collects only where interest consumes the property.
Ravina and Ameimar explain that Rabbi Yohanan's rule applies to widows, and the marriage contract is paid for the wife's favor.
Rav Nahman says he would not collect from orphans for an ordinary debt until he heard Rav Huna's ruling in Rav's name.
Asks why Rav Nahman initially would not collect payment from minor orphans.
Rav Pappa says collecting a debt is a mitzva orphans need not perform, and Rav Huna says the father may have paid by coin bundles.
Asks what practical difference lies between these two explanations.
The difference shows when the father admits the debt or dies under excommunication, where Rav Huna collects but Rav Pappa does not.
Eretz Yisrael's ruling: the collections apply where the father died under excommunication, and the halakha follows Rav Huna.

ranges.en: Asks whether the mishna on proclaiming orphans' property concerns a gentile creditor, and concludes it must concern a Jewish creditor.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua can read the mishna as a father admitting nonpayment, but this leaves Rav Pappa's view with a difficulty.
Rav Pappa can say the mishna concerns a marriage contract paid for favor, or a gentile creditor who accepted Jewish law for thirty days.
Objects that a creditor who accepted Jewish law should also wait until the orphans reach majority.
Brings a baraita on proclaiming a sale for a marriage contract or a creditor as a source for the same question.
Presses that on Rav Pappa's view, a sale to pay a creditor, not for favor, still poses a difficulty.
The baraita concerns a gentile creditor who accepted Jewish law for thirty days but not for waiting until majority.
Rava says the court does not collect from orphans' property out of fear of an unseen receipt from their father.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objects that a mishna lets a wife collect by oath, so receipts are not feared.
Rabbi Aha Sar HaBira reports a ruling of Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha at Antioch, and Rabba reports Rav Nahman allowing creditors to collect by oath.
Rav Huna asks why, if receipts are feared, Rava does not apply the same concern to a debtor overseas.
Rava says there is no concern for a receipt here, so people do not take others' money and settle overseas.
Rava rules that the court does not collect a father's debt from orphans, except when the father directs payment of a named item.
The Sages of Neharde'a hold the court collects and appoints a steward in all such cases, except for a field the witnesses show is not the father's.
Rav Ashi summarizes the halakha: no collection for a standard loan, and a steward is appointed where the father directed payment.

ranges.en: Mishna: one who consecrates his property while owing his wife's marriage contract; Rabbi Eliezer requires a vow against benefit, Rabbi Yehoshua does not.
Asks on what principle Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree.
Rabbi Eliezer thinks a person would collude even against the Temple treasury, while Rabbi Yehoshua thinks he would not.
Challenges this with Rav Huna's ruling that a deathbed consecration is believed, implying no collusion, so the dispute must be elsewhere.
Replies that the dispute concerns a healthy person, while all agree about the dying; alternative readings concern a public vow.
Asks why Ameimar's distinction about public and consented vows does not settle the dispute.
The dispute is instead about requesting dissolution of a vow involving consecrated property.
Baraita with the same dispute, adding that Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon ties each view to Beit Shammai or Beit Hillel.
Restates Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's parallel ruling about a guarantor of a marriage contract.
Narrative: Rav Huna's financial strait, and Abaye's advice that he divorce his wife so her claim falls on the guarantor.
Rava objects that the mishna requires a vow in such a case, so the advice cannot work for a wife who remarries.
Abaye replies that one may divorce outside court to avoid a vow; Rav Huna is later revealed to be a priest, so poverty followed him.
Asks whether Abaye really said this, since he calls one who advises selling a benefactor's property a wicked person.
Abaye's advice concerned a son, and a Torah scholar, which are different cases.
Objects that Abaye could simply say the guarantor of a marriage contract is not liable at all.

ranges.en: Asks how the marriage contract could be collected from Moshe bar Atzrei if Rav Huna had no property at the time of the loan.
Either Rav Huna had property when his father guaranteed, or a father guarantees for his son even without the son's property.
Cites the dispute on guarantors and kablanim, and holds that a guarantor of a marriage contract does not bind himself as a mitzva.
Asks whether a buyer of a husband's sold property is liable to the vow requirement when the wife collects from him.
Rav Pappa replies that the tanna did not list every case, and a buyer falls under the same reasoning.
The Sages of Neharde'a hold the vow applies only to what the mishna lists, so no vow is needed for buyers.
Explains the Neharde'a reasoning: the vow protects Temple profit and the guarantor's mitzva, but a buyer knowingly took on the risk.
Mishna: a consecrated estate with a wife's contract and a creditor's debt is redeemed cheaply by lending a small extra amount.
Asks why the mishna needs to say the property is redeemed, rather than given directly to the creditor.
Baraita of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: redemption on this basis applies only when the debt equals the consecrated value, which the mishna does not follow.
Asks how far the property must cover the debt, according to the Rabbis, for this redemption to apply.
Rav Sheshet says the consecrated property must be worth at least half the debt, otherwise it is redeemed at its value.
Mishna: an indebted valuation-obligor keeps thirty days of food, twelve months of clothing and tools, with the craftsman and farmer rules, and a consecrator loses even his phylacteries.
Asks what reason the verse gives for letting the debtor keep these tools.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reads the verse if he be too poor for your valuation as an instruction to sustain the vower from the valuation money.
Mishna: food and garments are left for the vower, but not for his wife or children.
Asks the reason: the verse sustains only him from the valuation, not his wife and children.
Mishna: Rabbi Eliezer says a farmer keeps his pair of oxen and a donkey driver keeps his donkey.
The Rabbis say these animals are not tools of the trade but property, so they are repossessed.
Asks whether it is obvious that one saw suffices when many adzes can be sold to buy another saw.
Needed because after repossession no one will lend him a tool, so the treasurer must help him obtain the extra tool.
Mishna: a consecrator of all his property loses his phylacteries to the treasury.
Narrates Rav Yeimar ordering a seller's phylacteries removed and given to the buyer as part of the property.
Asks what this incident teaches, since the mishna already states the rule.
Restates the mishna: phylacteries of a consecrator are taken.
Needed because one might think consecration differs from sale, since a person would not sell a mitzva item without saying so.
Mishna: neither the wife's nor the children's clothes, dyed garments or new sandals are repossessed.
Mishna: the treasury values items at their present location and price, not at the higher price a buyer might get elsewhere.
Baraita: the verse as of that day shows the pearl is appraised where it is; unspecified consecration goes to Temple upkeep.
Mishna: an ancestral field may not be consecrated less than two years before the Jubilee, nor redeemed less than one year after.
A baraita seems to contradict the mishna, allowing consecration before the Jubilee year and denying it during the Jubilee year itself.
Rav and Shmuel: the mishna refers to consecration for redemption at a reduced price, which must not be done less than two years before the Jubilee.
Rav holds a field consecrated during the Jubilee year is consecrated and redeemed at full value; Shmuel holds it is not consecrated at all.
Rav Yosef objects, using an a fortiori argument, and cites Rabbi Yehuda's mishna to show the inference fails.
Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon, who says priests enter the field without paying, so the a fortiori inference holds.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav holds that the field returns to the priests, not the owner, so no a fortiori inference is needed from the Jubilee.
Asks why Rav reads the verse to include the Jubilee year itself, and how Shmuel answers that the verse says from the Jubilee.
Objects to Rav from a baraita that a field consecrated in the Jubilee year is not consecrated, and draws a contrary inference from Rav's reply.
Rav replies the baraita follows the Rabbis, and his own view follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who includes the first and seventh days.
Asks what the extra pundeyon per year is for, if Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that the Jubilee year is included.
Objects that a baraita says Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi requires a sela and a pundeyon per year, which would not fit the inclusion view.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi follows Rabbi Yehuda, who counts the fiftieth year in both cycles, leaving forty-nine years per cycle.
Presses Shmuel: if Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi follows the Rabbis, the pundeyon arithmetic must be different, so the mishna should say that.
Brings a mishna forbidding redemption less than a year after the Jubilee, to support Shmuel's reading.
Asks, on Rav's view, what the mishna's after the Jubilee year means.
Asks whether the mishna means the actual year after the Jubilee, and suggests the phrase refers to something else.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the mishna's point: a partial year in the middle of the Jubilee cycle is not deducted, so one pays the full sela and pundeyon.
Asks what the tanna is teaching, since the no-month-counting rule is stated again explicitly in the next clause.
Mishna: one does not count months to lower the price owed to the Temple treasury, though the treasury may count them to raise it.
Baraita: the verse says to reckon years, not months, and lets the priest count months only at his discretion.
Mishna: the field-size and crevice rules, and the sela-and-pundeyon per remaining year rule, with the owner's one-fifth surcharge.
Baraita, with Levi, on the measure of a homer of barley seed: the sowing is measured by hand, at an average density.
Suggests crevices should be consecrated alone, then rejects this with a baraita reading the word field as covering any size.
Mar Ukva says the crevices in the mishna are full of water and not fit for sowing, so they are not measured with the field.
Asks why crevices under ten handbreadths are measured with the field, if they are unfit for sowing.
Mishna: a field consecrated two or three years before the Jubilee is redeemed at a sela and a pundeyon per year.
Baraita on the verse and a deduction shall be made: years passed since consecration are also deducted.
Mishna: an owner who asks to pay year by year is not heard, and must pay the whole sum at once.
Baraita: the word the money shows the sum must be paid as one payment, with the owner's surcharge alone.
Mishna: the field's Jubilee status depends on who redeemed it, and a priest who redeemed it does not keep it.

ranges.en: Baraita opens by quoting the verses on an unredeemed field and a field sold to another
Asks whether the verse excludes the son or only a sold field to a different person
Explains that a man refers to a brother, so another must mean someone other than a son
Asks what justifies including the son and excluding the brother
Son stands in the father's place for designating a maidservant and for inheriting a Hebrew slave
On the contrary, the brother should be included since he takes the place in levirate marriage
Levirate marriage applies only without a son, so a son replaces the father more than a brother
Why need this answer, since two justifications for the son already exist against one for the brother
The slave rule is not written explicitly; the levirate refutation is the basis for the conclusion
Rabba bar Avuh asks whether a daughter preserves a consecrated field for her father
Brings a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael to show a daughter counts as another when a son exists
Rabbi Zeira asks which heir can redeem a field a woman consecrated for her
The dilemma is left unresolved, so it stands as a tie
Rami bar Hama asks about a field consecrated less than two years before the Jubilee
Rav Hisda asks Rami what his reasoning is
Rami's reasoning: a deduction verse implies only fields fit for deduction go to priests
On the contrary, the verse shows any unredeemed field goes to the priests
Cites the Jubilee verse to show a field consecrated under two years is also fit for redemption
Cites the mishna case of a priest who redeemed the field and it reached the Jubilee
A baraita opens by quoting the verse that the ancestral field is the priest's
Asks what the verse adds with the phrase about the ancestral possession
Explains the derivation: a priest may not claim a redeemed field as his own by a fortiori reasoning
A fortiori conclusion, and the verse's 'ancestral possession' shows the field is not his own
Asks how the field is treated
It leaves his hand and is divided among all the priests, his brethren
Mishna: priests enter an unredeemed field at the Jubilee and pay its redemption price, per Rabbi Yehuda
Rabbi Shimon: priests enter the field but do not pay the redemption price
Rabbi Eliezer: priests never enter; the field becomes an abandoned field until a non-priest redeems it
Asks the basis for Rabbi Yehuda's view that priests must pay the redemption price
Derives it by verbal analogy from holy-house consecration, redeemable only for money
Asks the source for Rabbi Shimon's view that the field is given free
Derives it by verbal analogy from the Shavuot lambs given to priests for free
Asks why Rabbi Yehuda does not also derive his view from the Shavuot lambs
One derives rules for Temple-maintenance property like an ancestral field from the Temple's upkeep items

ranges.en: Asserts that the halakha of Temple maintenance items is not derived from consecrated altar items, with the house example.
Objects that Rabbi Shimon should derive the rule from a consecrated house, then explains why that analogy fails.
Presents Rabbi Eliezer's position that priests neither enter the consecrated field nor pay its redemption.
Rabba asks for the reason behind Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.
Rabba answers by reading the verses in Leviticus 27 as two separate halakhot.
Abaye rejects Rabba's reading, since a sharp knife cannot cut the verses out of order.
Abaye offers a baraita reading of anymore to support Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning.
Asks which Jubilee cycle the verse refers to, and concludes it must be the second.
Challenges whose opinion the baraita follows, since Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon cannot fit it.
Concludes that the baraita is Rabbi Eliezer's, and that his reason comes from the word anymore.
Challenges whether the baraita can be read that way, asking what Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon derive from anymore.
Explains the baraita in line with their views, using a field consecrated by a priest and then redeemed.
Raises a hypothetical reading that the verse anymore is meant to refute.
Brings a baraita on the verse to the one from whom it was bought, to show the field returns to the treasurer.
Asks why the verse must first say to the one from whom it was bought, if the next phrase suffices.
Explains the first phrase refers to a field returning to the priest who sold it.
States that the Torah needed both phrases, despite apparently teaching the same halakha.
Explains that without the to-the-seller phrase, one would think a priest-sold field could return to its original owner.

Asks why the second halakha is needed, since it is identical to the halakha for houses.
Teaches the lamb and house halakhot derive from each other by a verbal analogy of year.
Mishna: where the seller says a full year, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gives the seller a year plus its intercalated addition.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi counts 365 days, while the Rabbis count twelve months and any intercalated month benefits the seller.
Mishna: if the twelve months pass without redemption, the house becomes the buyer's permanently.
Baraita: the word permanently teaches it is absolute, and also includes a house given as a gift.
Asks the reason the verse uses the expanded term permanently, rather than the shorter form.
The Sages cite the baraita before Rav Pappa.
Asks whether the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, who says a gift is not like a sale.
Rav Pappa: even if the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, here the word permanently explicitly includes a gift.
Objects that the Jubilee verse also includes a gift, which Rabbi Meir does not include, so the baraita cannot follow him.
Baraita: a house consecrated in walled cities may always be redeemed, and if not redeemed by month twelve, it is permanently the other's.
Asks from where this matter is derived.
Shmuel: the verse for him the buyer's, even from Temple treasury, and throughout his generations excludes the Temple treasury.
Asks why the verse needs it shall not go out in the Jubilee, after saying permanently.
Rav Safra: it teaches that a house sold in a Jubilee year during the sale year does not return to its owner in the Jubilee.
Mishna: formerly the buyer concealed himself until month twelve passed, so Hillel instituted that the seller deposits money in the court chamber.
Rava infers from Hillel's ordinance that a conditional divorce is valid only if the wife gives the money with the husband's consent.

ranges.en: Infers from Hillel's ordinance that giving against the recipient's will is not generally considered giving.
Rav Pappa objects: Hillel's ordinance may apply only where the seller repays when the buyer is absent.
Rava's parallel version: a divorce conditioned on payment, where the wife pays with or against his will, is a valid giving.
Rav Pappa objects again: perhaps only consent makes it valid, and Hillel instituted the ordinance for buyers hiding at year's end.
Mishna: an area within the city wall is like a walled city's houses, with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagreeing on fields and on a house built into the wall.
Baraita derives from the word house, excluding fields, that outbuildings and other structures inside the city are included, per Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Meir derives the same structures from the verse, and also includes fields inside the city.
Objects that the word house is written, so how can Rabbi Meir include fields?
Rav Ḥisda, citing Rav Ketina: the word house excludes fields; Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda dispute only quarries and sand beds.
Baraita: Rabbi Meir holds quarries and sand beds are like houses, while Rabbi Yehuda holds they are like fields.
Rabbi Yehuda holds a house built into the wall is not like a walled city's house, while Rabbi Shimon holds the outer wall counts.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: both sides derive from the verse about Rahab's house on the wall, reading it literally or as residing on the wall.
Mishna: a city whose houses form its wall, or that lacks a Joshua-era wall, is not a walled city; lists the walled cities.
Baraita: a city with a wall, not a wall of roofs or a surrounding white wall, is excluded, except Tiberias, whose sea is a wall.
Rabbi Eliezer bar Yosei: the verse which has a wall reads as lo, so a city that once had a wall keeps its status.
Lists the mishna's walled cities and the baraita's location of Gamla, Gedod, Ḥadid, Ono and Jerusalem.
Asks what the tanna intends, whether these are the only walled cities in the Galilee, Transjordan and Judea.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye: the baraita lists the walled cities of the Galilee, Transjordan and Judea, each surrounded by a Joshua-era wall.
Rava: the baraita specifies which Gamla, Gedod, Ḥadid and Ono are meant, since other lands have no such cities.
Asks whether a house in Jerusalem is transferred in perpetuity after a year, given a baraita says it is not.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: the mishna refers to cities like Jerusalem, where houses are transferred permanently, unlike Jerusalem itself.
Rav Ashi: perhaps there were two places called Jerusalem in Judea, one where the rule applies, as with two Kadeshes.
Baraita: the Sages counted those cities because the returning exiles found and sanctified them; Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei holds sanctity was temporary.
Objects from a baraita quoting Deuteronomy 3 that these cities cannot be the only walled cities, since sixty cities were fortified.
Asks whether the baraita can mean the exiles sanctified these cities, given it later says they need not be sanctified.
Baraita: any city with a tradition of a Joshua-era wall keeps its mitzvot, since the initial sanctity of the land was eternal.
Two tanna'im may dispute Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei, or a baraita is by Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei on lo having a wall.
Asks the reason for the opinion that the initial sanctity was only temporary.
Nehemiah: the exiles made sukkot as had not been done since Joshua, so the verse cites Ezra's arrival as Joshua's.
The verse compares the return in Ezra's days to Joshua's days, when Sabbatical and Jubilee years were counted and walled cities sanctified.
Deuteronomy 30:5 compares your possession to your fathers' possession, so the renewal of the mitzvot applies to the return.
Asks how the tanna holding that the initial sanctity is eternal reads the Nehemiah verse.
Ezra's prayer against idolatry protected them like a sukka; the verse faults Joshua for not praying, as Moses lacked Eretz Yisrael's merit.
Asks why Deuteronomy's word and you shall possess it does not show the land needed sanctifying again.
Asks whether the Jubilee was counted in Ezra's time, given it was nullified when the tribes were exiled.
Baraita: Jubilee was nullified when Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh were exiled, per Leviticus 25:10, to all its inhabitants.
Baraita: the Jubilee does not apply when the tribes are intermingled, since the verse says all its inhabitants in proper arrangement.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: they counted Jubilee years only to sanctify the Sabbatical cycle, not for Jubilee laws to take effect.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that if the fiftieth year counts for both cycles, there is no need to count Jubilees, so the baraita must not follow Rabbi Yehuda.
Asks whether the Sabbatical and Jubilee years were counted after the exile, citing Jeremiah's verse on freeing Hebrew slaves.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the verse concerns two kinds of slave, and Jeremiah's words are reproof, so the Jubilee was then in effect.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: the Jubilee lapsed with the exile, but Jeremiah returned the tribes, and Josiah ruled over them.
Derives Jeremiah's return of the tribes from Ezekiel's verse that the seller shall not return to what he sold.
Derives Josiah's rule over the ten tribes from the verse about the tomb at Bethel.
Asks what Josiah, king of Judah, has to do with the altar at Bethel in the kingdom of Israel.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak derives the return of the tribes from Hosea's verse on a harvest for Judah.
Mishna: houses of unwalled courtyards have the redemption rules of walled-city houses, and leave the buyer in the Jubilee like fields.
Baraita: the verse juxtaposes unwalled courtyard houses to ancestral fields, so both leave the buyer in the Jubilee.
Baraita: they are redeemable at once, and yet leave the buyer in the Jubilee, per the verse they shall go out.
Asks what the tanna means in the last clause, given ancestral fields leave the buyer in the Jubilee.
Rav Huna: the verse concerns a house consecrated and redeemed by another, which must return in the Jubilee.
Rav Huna compares the case to walled-city houses and to consecrated ancestral fields, so the verse is needed to resolve it.
Rav Zeira objects: why specify a redemption by another, since the house should return even unredeemed.
Abaye: an unredeemed house does not return in the Jubilee, so consecrated property does not leave without redemption.
Derives from the Levite, whose consecrated property leaves the Temple treasury only by redemption, that an Israelite's does too.
Asks from where the Levite rule is derived, that his consecrated property does not leave without redemption.
Baraita on the verse of a Levite's sold house: sold items return free, but consecrated property returns only with redemption.
Rav Huna disagrees with Rabbi Oshaya, who holds that a redeemer becomes owner in all regards.
The verse on the field of the Jubilee specifies a field, so only a field leaves the Temple treasury to the priests.
Asks why the verse says they shall go out in the Jubilee, given Rabbi Oshaya's view.
Rav Pappa: needed for a seller of an unwalled courtyard house when the Jubilee arrives in the second year.
Rav Pappa elaborates by comparing the case to walled-city houses and to sold ancestral fields, which need a further year.
A baraita follows Rav Huna and refutes Rabbi Oshaya: a consecrated unwalled-courtyard house returns in the Jubilee if not redeemed.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: two courtyards each with two houses are unwalled, even if a Joshua-era wall surrounds the city.
Baraita infers from the verse on houses of courtyards the minimum count of two houses and two courtyards.
Mishna: an Israelite or Levite who inherits a walled-city house from a maternal grandfather of the other status follows different rules, per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis.
Asks like whom an Israelite who inherits from a Levite maternal grandfather redeems, if the rule is only for Levite sellers.
Explains the mishna means he redeems only under the standard one-year procedure, except when the seller is a Levite in Levite cities.
Asks from where it is derived that the seller must also be a Levite, not merely the house located in a Levite city.
Baraita: the verse from the Levites, read twice, shows some Levites may always redeem, excluding mamzer and Gibeonite Levites.
The Rabbis hold the rule applies to any heir of a Levite-city portion, even if he is not a Levite.
Mishna: Levite cities may not turn a field into an empty lot or an empty lot into a field, nor a city into an empty lot.
Rabbi Elazar: this applies to Levite cities, while in Israelite cities one may change a field to an empty lot to avoid destroying them.
Mishna: priests and Levites may always sell and redeem their houses and fields.
Cites the verse: the Levites shall have a perpetual right of redemption, which also includes priests as members of Levi.
Rabbi Elazar's qualification restated: in Levite cities the rule is stricter, which everyone agrees on.
Asks from where these matters are derived, per Rabbi Elazar.
Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse that the field of their cities shall not be sold, meaning it may not be changed.
Objects that if it means not sold at all, this conflicts with the verse that Levites' redemption is perpetual, implying sale.
Rather, not sold means not changed: the field, empty lot or city keeps its status.
Priests and Levites may sell always and redeem always.
Baraita: the perpetual redemption of Levites is needed to exclude the two-year limit and the Jubilee leaving rule for their fields.
Baraita: the verse on a Levite's consecrated field shows it is not transferred to priests but may be redeemed always.
Baraita: the verse on a house in a walled city shows a Levite may always redeem his walled-city house.
Asks why the verse excludes Levites' houses in walled cities, given a baraita says Levite cities may not be walled.
Rav Kahana: the baraita forbidding walls refers to a city first walled then settled, and the other to one settled first then walled.
Asks whether a city first settled and later walled counts as walled, given a baraita on this distinction.
Verse and baraita: a house in a walled city means one walled first then settled, not one settled then walled.
Baraita derives from a verbal analogy with the verse on gentiles that walls must have been built by gentiles before the conquest.
Rav Yosef son of Rav Sala Ḥasida: the first baraita concerns a city walled then settled by Levites, lots of walled cities fell to Levites.

ranges.en: Objection that the city and its lots would be dismantled, so it cannot count as walled.
Rav Ashi replies that the baraita is needed so Levites may always redeem houses sold in such cities.
The Sages teach a baraita on the case of a priest's consecrated field.
The baraita cites Leviticus 27:21 as its source text.
Asks what the superfluous phrase "as a field dedicated" is meant to teach.
Explains the verse excludes a priest arguing that the field is already his.
States the priest's a fortiori argument that the verse rejects.
Brings a verse to refute the a fortiori argument and settle the rule.
Asks what the baraita can learn from the dedicated field if the rule is already known.
Explains the baraita teaches a rule by juxtaposing the dedicated field to the ancestral field.
Derives the rule by analogy: the priest's dedicated field leaves his hands at the Jubilee like an Israelite's ancestral field.
Gemara objects that the two cases are not comparable, since the priest only takes a share.
Rami bar Ḥama defends the verse's necessity, comparing the dedicated field to hallowed things.
Objects that hallowed things are not in the priest's possession, so the comparison fails.
Rav Naḥman replies that the verse is needed for a different reason.
Presents the hypothetical view that a priest may always redeem a consecrated ancestral field.
Cites Leviticus 25:34 on perpetual possession as the basis of that view.
Concludes the field stays with the priest only if it is his ancestral field, and closes the chapter.
